If it's flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off: a flashing light means a severe misfire that can overheat the catalytic converter and start a fire. Do the same if it's steady but the engine shakes hard, loses power or smells of fuel. If it's steady and the car drives normally, drive gently and get it checked soon.

A flashing or blinking check engine light is more serious than a steady one. It means the engine is misfiring badly and unburned fuel is passing into the exhaust, which can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter in a matter of minutes. Ease off the gas, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't keep driving; have it towed or checked before you go further.
Stop driving as soon as it's safe
No. Pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off. Driving even a few miles can destroy the engine.

On some cars the light flickers or blinks instead of staying on, typically at idle, when braking or going round a bend. That pattern often means the oil level is low enough that the pump briefly sucks air as the oil sloshes away from the pickup, though a failing pump or sensor can do it too. It is still a stop-and-check light, not a glitch, and it usually turns solid if you keep driving.
Stop driving as soon as it's safe
Not if it's red. Pull over, turn the engine off and let it cool. Driving an overheating engine can warp the cylinder head or blow the head gasket.

On some European cars a blinking coolant symbol means low coolant and a steady one means the engine is too hot, but makes differ and a flashing red light can also mean overheating. Either way, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off, and check the owner's manual for what your car's light means.
Pull over when it's safe

Turn off the A/C, radio, seat heaters and anything else you don't need, and pull over somewhere safe. If the temperature gauge is high or the steering feels heavy, turn the engine off and call for help. If not, check your owner's manual: some makers say to keep the engine running because it may not restart. The car is running on battery alone and can stall within minutes, so don't try to finish your trip.

On some cars it flickers or glows dimly at idle and then goes out when you rev the engine or start driving. That points to a charging system that is only just keeping up, usually a slipping drive belt or an alternator on the way out, and it should be tested before it fails completely.
Stop driving as soon as it's safe
Release the parking brake first. If the light stays on, don't drive until it's checked. Low brake fluid can mean a leak and brakes that may not stop the car.
Get it checked soon

If the red BRAKE light is on too, or the pedal feels soft or different, stop driving and have it towed. With only the amber ABS light on, normal braking usually still works but the wheels can lock in a hard stop, so drive gently to a shop, leave extra stopping distance and avoid wet or icy roads.
Have it checked right away
The car drives normally, but the airbags and seat belt pretensioners may not work in a crash. Have it checked right away, and check for open airbag recalls with your VIN.

On some older Honda, Toyota and Subaru models the light blinks in a repeating pattern instead of staying solid. The number of blinks is a code the system is trying to tell you, and a shop reads that pattern or the stored code to find the faulty part. A blinking light is no less serious than a solid one.
Get it checked soon

If the light is red, pull over when it's safe and stop: on some cars red means a steering fault, not just lost assist. If it's amber and the steering feels normal, get it checked soon. If the steering takes more effort than normal, don't drive on: have it towed.
Get it checked soon

If it says the transmission is hot, pull over when it's safe and do what the message or your owner's manual says: some cars want you to idle in Park, others to turn the engine off. Otherwise drive gently and get it checked soon; ignoring it can turn a small fix into a new transmission.

A flashing gear symbol, or a flashing D, D4 or O/D OFF indicator, nearly always means the transmission computer has stored a fault and has put the car into a protected mode. Treat a flashing light as more urgent than a steady one, keep your speed down and stay off the accelerator.
Get it checked soon

Check the level as soon as the engine is cool, before you drive further. If the light is red or says stop, or the temperature gauge is climbing, pull over and turn the engine off. If it's amber and the tank is only a little low, top it up and get the leak checked soon.
Get it checked soon

Read the message on the dash first; the message decides, not the triangle. Anything about oil, engine temperature, brakes or steering means stop somewhere safe and turn the engine off. Door ajar, washer fluid and key battery messages are reminders. On makes that show a red triangle, treat it as stop and get help.

On some Toyota and Lexus models the triangle flashes instead of staying on, but it means the same thing: a message is waiting on the screen. Flashing is not more urgent than steady here. The message decides how serious it is.
Get it checked soon

If the screen tells you to stop, the car loses power, or you smell burning, pull over somewhere safe, turn the car off and call for help. Don't touch any orange cables. Otherwise drive gently and straight to a shop that works on hybrids. Power may suddenly be limited, so stay off the highway if you can and don't start a long trip.
Get it checked soon
Refill the DEF (diesel exhaust fluid) soon. If the dash shows a countdown to reduced speed or a no-restart warning, act right away, because the truck will limit itself when it reaches zero.

On some trucks and cars the light stops being steady and starts flashing, or the message changes to a mileage countdown, when the tank is nearly empty or the system has a fault. Treat a flashing light or a countdown as urgent: once the countdown runs out the vehicle will limit itself to a crawl.
Get it checked soon

If it's the only light on and the engine runs normally, a 20-minute drive at a steady highway speed usually lets the filter clean itself. If the light stays on, flashes, or the engine loses power, get it checked before the filter clogs.

On several makes a flashing or blinking filter light, or the same light paired with a check engine light, means the filter is badly blocked and the vehicle can no longer clean it by itself. At that point driving on the highway will not fix it and you need a shop before the engine goes into reduced power.
Get it checked soon

On dry, normal roads the car usually still drives, but four-wheel drive may not work. Avoid snow, mud, steep grades and towing until it's checked. If it came on with a clunk, grinding or the car feels like it's binding in turns, stop and get it checked.

A blinking 4WD symbol usually means the system is trying to shift and has not made it, so it is stuck part way between two-wheel and four-wheel drive. On some trucks it also blinks when the transfer case has got hot from spinning the wheels and the system has shut itself down to cool off.
Get it checked soon

If you hear grinding or metal scraping when you brake, or the pedal feels different, stop driving and have it towed: the pads are worn through. Otherwise the light usually comes on with a little pad left, so book a brake check in the next few days and drive gently with extra stopping distance until then.
Get it checked soon

If the light is red, or an oil can symbol comes on with a buzzer or a STOP ENGINE message, pull over safely and turn the engine off. With the amber oil level warning, keep any trip short and gentle and add the correct oil today, because low oil turns into low oil pressure and engine damage.
Get it checked soon

If a rear wheel drags, smells hot or the car won't move freely, stop and have it towed on a flatbed. Otherwise short trips are usually possible, because this brake mainly holds the car when it's parked. Expect it not to hold on a slope: leave the car in Park, or in gear on a manual, and follow your owner's manual for parking on hills.

On some cars the parking brake light blinks rather than staying on. A blinking light means the brake has not finished applying or releasing, so the car is not being held properly. Set it and release it once more, and if it keeps blinking, do not leave the car on a slope relying on it.
Get it checked soon

If the car still accelerates normally, drive it gently and book a shop within a day or two. If power is held back, the engine will not rev freely and the car may feel flat or stuck in gear: stay off the highway, and drive slowly straight to a shop or have it towed. If EPC appears with a red light, with the brake lights not working, or with heavy shaking, stop and get it looked at before going further.
Get it checked soon

If the red brake warning light comes on with it, or the pedal feels soft or long, stop driving and have it towed. Otherwise braking usually still works, but nothing will catch a skid and you get no extra boost in an emergency stop, so drive gently and get it checked within a few days.

The ESP BAS letters stay on steady. The skidding-car light beside them flashing while you drive is a different thing: that is stability control actually catching a slide, which is the system working, not a fault.
Get it checked soon

If it is flashing, or the car has dropped into reduced power, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off: a flashing light means a misfire that can overheat the exhaust. If it's steady and the car feels normal, drive gently and get it checked soon.

A flashing exhaust light means the engine is misfiring right now and unburned fuel is pouring into the catalytic converter, which can overheat it and start a fire. Pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't keep driving; have it towed or checked before you go further.
Release it. If it stays on, stop driving

Release the parking brake fully. If the light goes out, it was just the parking brake. If it stays on with the brake released, or the pedal feels soft or sinks toward the floor, stop driving and have the brakes checked or the car towed.

On some cars with a button-operated parking brake, the red light blinks instead of staying steady. A blinking light means the brake has not finished clamping or has not fully let go, so the car may not be held safely. Set it again, and if it keeps blinking, do not rely on it to hold the car on a slope.
Get it checked soon

Read the message and your owner's manual first. Some diesels, such as Ram trucks, say to stop the engine and drain the water before restarting. If yours doesn't, keep it to a short, gentle drive to get it drained the same day, and stop if the engine runs rough, loses power or smokes.
Get it checked soon

Short answer: only as far as you need to. If the car drives and shifts normally you can finish a local trip and book a shop in the next day or two. If the pedal feels dead, the car will not pick up speed, or the gears bang and slip, stay off the highway and drive gently straight to a shop, or have it towed. Do not tow a trailer or load it up while this light is on.

If a red light or an EV or hybrid system warning comes on with it, or the car keeps losing power, pull over somewhere safe, turn the car off and call for help. Otherwise, power is being limited: move to the right lane, get off the highway when it's safe and don't try to pass. Charge the battery or let it cool down. Don't drive it. Have it towed to a shop.
